blocks.text: One should also compare what Bochart says about the verb דגר below, book III, Ch. XI, p. 409 and 415. Had J. D. Michaelis weighed this properly, I would hardly think he would have written what we now read in the Supplemm. ad Lex. Hebr. vol. II, p. 394, and in the Animadverss. Philologg. ad Ierem. XVII, 11. There he declares that the meaning to gather has been attributed to the verb דגר wholly falsely, chiefly because agreement with the Arabic نجر [njr] is lacking; and since someone might adduce the Chaldee dialect, he says that in the passages of the Chaldee version of the O. T. which Buxtorf gives in his Chaldee Lexicon under the word דגר, the notion of collecting was introduced from a false interpretation of the Hebrew word. But these are words, not arguments. And that the interpretation collecting is certain is proved by the Chaldee דְגוֹר, heap, plainly named from collecting, traces of which notion we find in the Arabic نغر [nghr], he snatched, seized. [II, 633] But on these points Michaelis is entirely silent, so that we may be all the more inclined to embrace his conjectures. He invents for himself this sequence of meanings, in the Supplemm. p. 396: "1) דגר, دجر [djr], he fled; hence 2) partridge, because of its very great speed in running [but for that very reason it could also be the ostrich]; and from this noun 3) the denominative to peep, or to cluck." Had someone else put forward such things, he would surely have been rightly and deservedly hissed off the stage by that very eminent man himself. Nor is דגר in Ierem. XVII, 11. a substantive, as Michaelis asserts. For the Pathach in the last syllable of the verb דגר is here lengthened to Cametz on account of the accent Paschta; and although this is unusual, it nevertheless happens sometimes even with the lesser accents. Buxtorf has collected examples in the Thesaurus Grammat. book II, ch. 23, p. 611.

Oedmann, in den Vermischten Sammlungen vol. II, p. 57 ff., takes it as certain that قارية [qāriya] is merops apiaster Linn. (Syst. T. 1, p. 460, ed. 13), because some of the things the Arabs say about قارية [qāriya] are also found in the merops, such as the green colour, the shortness of the legs, and the voice drawn back in the throat. But several things keep me from agreeing with that most learned man. First, the merops has a curved and compressed bill, whereas the bill of the Karia is long. Second, the قارية [qāriya] foretells rain, which no one has observed in the merops. Oedmann, however, wrongly twists what the Arabs relate of the قارية [qāriya], that it is a harbinger of rain, to mean that the bird arrives at the season of the year when the regular rains begin to fall in those regions; evidently so that a new similarity between the merops and the قارية [qāriya] might appear. But Oedmann's opinion is wholly overthrown by the fact that the Arabs say entirely different things about the merops apiaster, which they call شُقِرّاق [shuqirrāq] or شُرِقّاق [shuriqqāq], and أَخْيَل [akhyal] (to which names must be added وَرْوَار [warwār] Varvar, from its sharp bill; see Golius' Lexicon p. 2650 and Hasselquist's Travels p. 302). Bochart will give the passages in full from the Arabs below, book II, ch. 25, p. 298 ff.; whoever examines them will readily see that the قارية [qāriya] and the merops are entirely different birds. To mention a few points: they write that the bird أَخْيَل [akhyal] or شُرِقّاق [shuriqqāq] hunts bees, which they do not record of the قارية [qāriya]. Further, whereas the قارية [qāriya] is a bird of good omen, the merops is of ill omen. So even after Oedmann we are no better informed than by Bochart. But it is also doubtful whether the قارية [qāriya] is the same bird as the קרא; for what we read about this bird in the books of the ancient Hebrews and in the Talmudic writers is not enough to form a sure judgement on the matter; and what Oedmann adduces to show that קרא, like قارية [qāriya], is the merops apiaster is too contrived and far-fetched, and moreover, as we have seen, it is plainly false of the قارية [qāriya].

That the Alexandrians either read קָרָא קֹרֵא, or that ἐφώνησε [ephōnēse] crept in here from another version, is an empty conjecture of Schleusner on Michaelis' Animadverss. in Ierem. Michaelis also made some remarks on the ancient versions in the Supplemm. vol. II, p. 394, under the word דגר, but such that they can be corrected from Bochart.
Franciscus Junius, with whom Louis de Dieu largely agrees.
Among the birds of Eretz Yisrael and Egypt Hasselquist lists a certain species of Charadrius, related to the herons, whose Arabic name he writes as Kervan, p. 314.
